fatal_errors: The proposed Ti sputter coating does not reconstruct the liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.
The initial material, processing conditions, irradiation energy and fluence, and resulting architecture all conflict with the target study.
The claimed 15% conductivity improvement and selected service conditions have no supporting evidence.
The hypothesis omits the decisive bicontinuous RHEA–Cu structure, selective Ti extraction, and spontaneously formed W-rich interlayer.

It treats irradiation as a condition for composite thermal-conductivity improvement, whereas the target irradiation result came from He implantation of precursor dendrites as a proxy, not the finished composite.
explanation: The response addresses the broad engineering theme of reducing W/Cu interfacial defects and proposes a testable coated-versus-untreated comparison, but it does not scientifically reconstruct the hidden work. The target intervention was 1200 °C, 96 h liquid-metal dealloying of WTaVTi in molten Cu, producing aligned Cu channels, retained refractory-alloy ligaments, and a roughly 300 nm W-rich passivating interface. None of those central elements appears. The generic claim that better bonding could improve conductivity has limited conceptual overlap, but the Ti coating, 100 nm thickness, 300 °C deposition, 500 °C/10 MPa condition, 1 MeV irradiation, and 15% gain are unsupported. The falsification experiment can test the empirical coating claim, although it does not adequately distinguish reduced voiding from coating-induced changes and uses a 10% failure threshold inconsistent with the stated 15% prediction. With no cited prior evidence, the proposal is an unsupported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
